facts.text: Founded in 1963 by Holmes Perkins.
Gallery building opened in 1990, designed by Adèle Naudé Santos.
Has no permanent collection and mounts about twelve shows a year.
Staged the first museum shows of Andy Warhol, Laurie Anderson, Agnes Martin and Robert Indiana.
Founded by Lauren Addis in 2016.
Contemporary art gallery and custom picture frame shop showing regional emerging artists.
Built in 1764 for Rebecca Rawle, a Quaker widow.
Fairmount Park Commission bought the house in 1869.
Placed on the National Register of Historic Places on March 24, 1972.
Stewarded since 1976 by Women for Greater Philadelphia.
Built from 1799 to 1800 by merchant Henry Pratt.
Named for the citrus fruits Pratt grew on the property.
Stands on land once part of Robert Morris's estate, The Hills.
First estate incorporated into Fairmount Park, in 1855.
Opened to the public on May 6, 2023, after a five-year renovation.
Housed in the former Barnes Foundation building designed by Paul Cret, home to the Barnes collection from 1925 to 2011.
Named for Frances M. Maguire, whose family gave a $50 million gift to the university in 2018.
Has served the community for over 75 years as an art school and gallery.
Offers up to ten exhibitions a year, including seasonal fine crafts shows.
Active since 1953 as an arts and humanities organization.
Housed in a historic carriage house in Roxborough.
Run entirely by volunteers and offers classes in drawing, painting, clay and fibers.
Built in 1926 to 1928 by the firm Mellor, Meigs & Howe.
Named for Marjorie Walter Goodhart of the Bryn Mawr class of 1912.
Houses McPherson Auditorium, Hepburn Teaching Theater and the Goodhart Music Room.

name: Marvin Samson Center for the History of Pharmacy

facts.text: Established in 1995 to coincide with the 175th anniversary of the Philadelphia College of Pharmacy.
Holds over 8,000 pharmaceutical and medical artifacts dating back to the 1600s.
Located on the first floor of Griffith Hall on the university's West Philadelphia campus.
Built in 1859 by Alan Wood, reportedly for his bride Mary.
Queen Anne Victorian style house.
Built between 1832 and 1834.
Oldest existing stock exchange building in the United States.
Philadelphia Stock Exchange's Board of Brokers moved in during 1834.
Now serves as headquarters of Independence National Historical Park.
Founded in 1984.
Specializes in 20th and 21st century art and design, especially the Studio Craft Movement.
Moved to the North American Street Arts Corridor in January 2025.
Built about 1761 to 1762 by privateer John Macpherson and his wife Margaret.
Builder-architect was Thomas Nevell.
Two small pavilions, an office and a summer kitchen, flank the main house.
Paint-your-own pottery and craft studio.
Hosts birthday parties, art clubs and offers pottery to-go kits.
Exhibits costumes and the history of the Mummers Parade, billed as America's oldest folk parade.
Artists' cooperative established in late 1977.
Members work in abstract, conceptual and representational forms.
Founded in 1986 and formerly called the Center for Art in Wood.
Permanent collection of about 1,200 handmade objects, from everyday items to sculpture.
Part of the global Museum of Illusions group.
Has more than 60 exhibits including holograms, stereograms and immersive rooms.
Occupies about 5,000 square feet.
Founded by publisher Irvin J. Borowsky and his daughter Gwen Borowsky.
Displays the 20-foot glass sculpture Flame of Liberty by Dale Chihuly.
Reopened March 1, 2025, after five years of renovation following a 2020 flood.
Houses the Muslim American Museum & Archive, focused on African American Muslim culture.
Part of an effort to revitalize the 4200 block of Lancaster Avenue.
Reconstruction of a 1791 building that served as the U.S. Department of War.
Original built by members of the Carpenters' Company.
Exhibits cover the Continental Army, Navy and Marine Corps.
Has a first-floor sculpture designed by Felix de Weldon.
Built as the home of William Rogers, powder master of the Nitre Hall powder mills.
Powder mills were built by Israel Whelen shortly after 1800.
Only intact building remaining from the valley's industrial era.
Home of the Haverford Township Historical Society collections, owned by the township.
Built in 1790 to 1791 in the Federal style.
Housed the U.S. Supreme Court from 1791 to 1800.
Served as Philadelphia's City Hall until 1854.
Architect was David Evans, Jr.
Georgian house of pink-red brick with a pillared front porch.
City bought it from Burd's heirs in 1869, making it part of Fairmount Park.
Maintained since 1982 by the volunteer Royal Heritage Society.
Established in 2010 by Jason Chen and Sara McCorriston.
Moved in 2023 into a 5-story, 7,000 square foot building.
Shows contemporary work by emerging and mid-career artists, with a focus on Philadelphia.
Designed by architect E. Allen Wilson in 1907 and built in 1911.
Paul Robeson lived here with his sister Marian Forsythe from 1966 until his death in 1976.
Owned and operated by the West Philadelphia Cultural Alliance.
First phase completed in 1899 to house finds from the Nippur expedition.
Rotunda with Harrison Auditorium completed in 1915.
Coxe Memorial Wing by Charles Klauder opened in 1926 for the Egyptian collection.
